c.tagline: Medieval walls, an imperial castle, and the world's most famous Christmas market.

emergency.note: 112 reaches ambulance and fire across the EU; 110 is the direct police line in Germany.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing in Christkindlesmarkt crowds and around the Hauptbahnhof late at night; otherwise usual awareness.

hood_desc: The southern half of the walled old town around the Hauptmarkt, St. Lorenz church and the main shopping streets; the most central, walkable base for first-timers.
The northern old town climbing to the Imperial Castle (Kaiserburg), with the Albrecht Dürer House, half-timbered lanes and the Weissgerbergasse; the historic sightseeing heart.
Nuremberg's bohemian, multicultural quarter just west of the walls, lined with indie shops, cafes, street art and artist studios; best for a youthful, creative vibe.
A busy, down-to-earth district just south of the main station around Aufsessplatz, with markets and cheap eats; a convenient budget base close to transport.
A leafy, well-heeled residential neighbourhood by the river with the Hesperides gardens and the historic Johannisfriedhof cemetery; quiet and green.

water.note: Tap water is excellent and safe to drink.

transit.hours: The U-Bahn runs roughly 4am-1am, later on weekends; NightLiner buses cover the small hours on Friday and Saturday nights.
transit.pay: No transit card needed: buy tickets in the VGN app or from station machines (bank cards accepted) and keep them for inspection. A single ride (Preisstufe A) is about €3.40 (~US$3.70) and a day ticket around €8.90; one ticket covers the U-Bahn, trams and buses. Staying weeks? The Deutschland-Ticket (€58/month) covers local transit nationwide.

food.name: Nurnberger Rostbratwurste
food.desc: Finger-sized pork sausages seasoned with marjoram, grilled over beechwood; protected by law and no longer than nine centimetres.

places.name: Bratwursthausle bei St. Sebald
places.note: Grills over an open beechwood fire beside the church; the city's best-known sausage house.

places.name: Bratwurst Roslein
places.note: Cavernous half-timbered hall claiming to be the world's largest bratwurst restaurant.

places.name: Zum Gulden Stern
places.note: Bills itself as the oldest bratwurst kitchen in the world, grilling in a 15th-century building.

food.name: Drei im Weggla
food.desc: Three grilled Nuremberg sausages jammed into a crusty roll with mustard - the standing-up street version, eaten in about a minute.

places.name: Bratwursthausle takeaway window
places.note: Hatch on the street sells them to go without queueing for a table.

places.name: Hauptmarkt grill stalls
places.note: Market-square stands grill sausages all day and through the Christmas market.

places.name: Bratwurst Roslein
places.note: Also does the roll version to take away from its street counter.

food.name: Schaufele
food.desc: Franconian pork shoulder slow-roasted in dark beer with caraway until the crackling shatters, served with a potato dumpling and gravy.

places.name: Zum Gulden Stern
places.note: Traditional Franconian roasts in a historic vaulted room a short walk from the sausage crowds.

places.name: Wirtshaus Hutt'n
places.note: Rustic wood-lined tavern with hearty Franconian roasts and a strong local following.

places.name: Bratwurst Roslein
places.note: Keeps Schaufele and other Franconian mains alongside the sausages.

food.name: Nurnberger Lebkuchen
food.desc: Spiced honey gingerbread on a thin wafer base, packed with nuts and candied peel; a protected Nuremberg product sold year-round.

places.name: Lebkuchen-Schmidt
places.note: Nuremberg's best-known Lebkuchen maker, with decorative tins that travel well as gifts.

places.name: Wicklein
places.note: Family firm baking Lebkuchen since 1615, with a shop right on the main square.

places.name: Christkindlesmarkt stalls
places.note: Dozens of Lebkuchen stands during the famous Christmas market, alongside gluhwein.

food.name: Blaue Zipfel
food.desc: Raw bratwursts poached in a vinegar, wine and onion broth until they turn pale blue-grey; sharp, light and served in the bowl.

places.name: Bratwursthausle bei St. Sebald
places.note: Serves the poached version for people who want the sausages without the grill smoke.

places.name: Zum Gulden Stern
places.note: Traditional Franconian preparation done in the old-fashioned sour broth.

places.name: Wirtshaus Hutt'n
places.note: Franconian tavern staple, good with a glass of local Silvaner.

food.name: Frankischer Sauerbraten
food.desc: Beef marinated for days in vinegar and spice then braised, the gravy thickened Franconian-style with gingerbread crumbs and raisins.

places.name: Wirtshaus Hutt'n
places.note: Old-school Franconian cooking with dumplings and red cabbage below the Kaiserburg.

places.name: Zum Gulden Stern
places.note: Regional classics beyond the sausages, cooked in a centuries-old kitchen.

food.name: Frankisches Rotbier
food.desc: Nuremberg's historic red-amber lager, maltier and darker than a helles, brewed in the city long before pale beer arrived.

places.name: Hausbrauerei Altstadthof
places.note: Brews Rotbier on site and runs tours of the rock-cut beer cellars beneath the Old Town.

places.name: Barfusser Hausbrauerei
places.note: Cellar brewpub near the station pouring its own unfiltered beers with Franconian food.

places.name: Wirtshaus Hutt'n
places.note: Good regional beer list to go with the roasts.

food.name: Franconian Silvaner
food.desc: Dry, earthy white wine from the Franconian vineyards up the Main, traditionally bottled in the flat green Bocksbeutel flask.

places.name: Zum Gulden Stern
places.note: Franconian wine by the glass and the flask alongside the grilled sausages.

places.name: Wirtshaus Hutt'n
places.note: Keeps regional Silvaner and Bacchus on a short, local wine list.

places.name: Bratwurst Roslein
places.note: Franconian wines poured in the big timbered hall as an alternative to beer.

landmarks: Kaiserburg (Imperial Castle)
The sandstone castle of the Holy Roman Emperors crowns the old town, its Sinwell Tower and ramparts surveying a sea of red roofs.
Hauptmarkt with Schöner Brunnen and Frauenkirche
Nuremberg's market square pairs a gilded fourteenth-century fountain, its wish-granting brass ring, with the Frauenkirche's noon mechanical clock show.
St. Lorenz Church
A twin-towered Gothic masterpiece sheltering Veit Stoss's suspended Annunciation carving and a fabled tabernacle spiraling twenty meters toward the vaults.
Albrecht Dürer House
The half-timbered home where the Renaissance master lived and worked from 1509 to 1528, now a museum with printing demonstrations.
Documentation Center Nazi Party Rally Grounds
A shard of glass and steel pierces Hitler's unfinished Congress Hall, unflinchingly examining the propaganda spectacle staged on these grounds.
Memorium Nuremberg Trials (Courtroom 600)
The actual courtroom where Nazi leaders faced justice in 1945-46, preserved with an absorbing exhibition on the trials' world-changing legacy.
Weißgerbergasse
Nuremberg's prettiest lane, a photogenic row of crooked half-timbered tanners' houses that survived the wartime bombing of the old town.
Germanisches Nationalmuseum
The German-speaking world's largest cultural-history museum, spanning Dürer paintings, the Behaim Globe and half a million treasures.
St. Sebaldus Church
The city's oldest parish church holds the bronze shrine of its patron saint, a Vischer workshop masterpiece ringed by medieval stained glass.
Henkersteg and the Pegnitz River Views
The covered wooden Hangman's Bridge and neighboring Weinstadel granary compose Nuremberg's most romantic river scene, glorious at dusk.

train.note: Trains leave from Nürnberg Hauptbahnhof, immediately outside the city walls and a two-minute walk from the Altstadt. Frequent ICE services reach Munich (~1h), Frankfurt (~2h), Berlin (~3h) and Würzburg, connecting to the full national high-speed network. There is no direct train to Prague - the standard route is the DB/CD IC Bus, which is booked as a train ticket and takes about 3h30. Cross-border fares to Austria are cheapest as a single Sparpreis Europa booking.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the ZOB beside Nürnberg Hauptbahnhof; Prague is a popular ~3h30 direct run. FlixBus tickets are online only and cheapest booked well ahead, and the DB IC Bus to Prague is sold through int.bahn.de as a rail ticket.

ferry.note: Nuremberg is landlocked, sitting on the small river Pegnitz and the Main-Danube Canal, so there are no passenger ferries. Small sightseeing boats operate on the canal and on the Wohrder See in summer, and river-cruise ships bound for the Danube pass through the canal locks nearby.
